title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without the rights holders' authorization. Udio ingested recorded music to build a generative model and deployed that model publicly before securing licenses from the labels that owned the recordings. The failure is located at the data-collection and training stage, before any user ever touched the product. A rights-clearance process applied before training began would have been the point at which this could have been caught.

The legal picture is still unresolved across multiple fronts. Universal Music Group settled and moved toward a licensing arrangement, Warner Music Group did the same, but Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging Udio copied more than 30,000 recordings, a court declined to allow Sony to expand an earlier case to include those recordings, and a class action by independent artists survived a dismissal attempt and was moved to a different jurisdiction. The musicians' union also brought its own action against Universal Music Group over the settlement itself. None of these suits has produced a final verdict, and the allegations in them are not findings of liability.

What is established is that a commercially deployed AI music system attracted simultaneous legal challenges from major labels, independent artists, and a performers' union, all centered on the same underlying question of whether copyrighted recordings may be used as training data without permission. The settlements reached so far converted that disputed use into a licensed one going forward, but they do not resolve what consequences, if any, attach to the training that already occurred.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group has settled a copyright lawsuit with AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve disputes over the company's use of copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, stream and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed. This marks the first major music licensing deal Udio has secured with a record label.

The original lawsuit claimed Udio used hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" to generate similar melodies without permission or compensation. Udio argued its AI learns from musical examples similar to how students study music. Under the new agreement, artists can opt into the platform and will receive compensation, though specific details remain undisclosed. Udio, launched in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am and Andreessen Horowitz, has attracted millions of users since its release.
